opus-5.5.text:
I think people often conflate these two, but they're really two different axes, and it helps to pull them apart.

Complexity is about a single task: how many steps it has, how precise the contact needs to be, how much the outcome depends on getting things right early, how much uncertainty there is in the environment. Folding a shirt, tying a knot, inserting a connector: these are complex because the state space is huge and errors compound over a long horizon.

Generality is about breadth: how many different tasks, objects, scenes, and embodiments a single system can handle without being re-engineered. A robot that can pick up ten thousand different objects in ten thousand kitchens is general, even if each individual pick is fairly simple.

For a long time the field traded one for the other. Classical robotics and a lot of early learning work went deep: you could get a beautifully engineered system that did one very complex thing, like assembling a specific part, but it was brittle the moment anything changed. The newer foundation-model approach went wide: large vision-language-action models trained on lots of diverse data can follow many instructions in many settings, but mostly on short, relatively simple, pick-and-place-style tasks.

My view is that the two aren't fundamentally opposed, but they're coupled through data and through representation. Complex tasks are really compositions of simpler skills plus the ability to recover when something goes wrong. If your system is general at the level of primitives (grasping, pushing, aligning, regrasping) and it has a good enough model of the world to plan and correct itself, then complexity becomes something you build on top of generality, not something you buy separately.

The catch is that this requires the right kind of data. Demonstrations of clean, successful short tasks give you breadth but not the long-horizon, failure-and-recovery experience that complex tasks require. So I think the next stage is less about collecting more of the same and more about getting data, whether from real robots, simulation, or human video, that covers long sequences, contact-rich interaction, and recovery from mistakes.

In short: generality is the foundation, complexity is the test. A truly general system should eventually show it can handle complex tasks, and a system that handles complex tasks only in one narrow setting hasn't really solved the problem. The goal is the intersection, and that's where I think the most interesting work is right now.

fable-5.1.text:
I think these two dimensions are often confused, but they're actually quite different axes, and the gap between them is where most of the hard questions in embodied intelligence live right now.

Complexity is about how hard a single task is: how many steps it involves, how precise the contact has to be, how long the horizon is, how much the system has to reason about physics or deformable objects. Something like folding a shirt or threading a cable is complex. Generality is about how many different tasks, objects, and environments one system can handle without being re-engineered. You can have very high complexity with almost no generality, which is basically what industrial robotics has been for decades: a robot arm doing an extremely precise, difficult task in a factory, but if you move the part two centimeters it fails.

What I find interesting is that for a long time the field assumed you climb complexity first and generality comes later. I actually think it's closer to the opposite. Generality is the foundation, and complexity gets layered on top of it. If you look at what happened in language and vision, the breakthrough wasn't that models got better at one hard task. It was that they got exposed to enough diversity that the representation itself became general, and then hard tasks became tractable because the model already understood the world well enough. For manipulation, the analogy is that a robot which has seen tens of thousands of different objects and scenes has a much better prior for picking up an object it has never seen than a robot trained to perfection on ten objects.

The catch is that in robotics, generality is far more expensive to acquire. Language has the internet. Robots don't have an internet of physical interaction. Every data point costs real time, real hardware, real wear. So there's a real tension: to get generality you need scale and diversity, but to get scale you tend to simplify the tasks you collect, which pulls down complexity. Most large robot datasets today are dominated by relatively simple pick-and-place because that's what you can collect at volume.

So my honest view is that the two aren't in conflict in principle, but they're in conflict in practice because of data economics. The groups that will make progress are the ones who find a way to get diverse data without paying full price for every sample. That means simulation that actually transfers, video and human demonstration as a weak signal, and models that can learn a general understanding of physical interaction from imperfect data, then fine-tune onto complex tasks with relatively little robot-specific data. If you get that recipe right, I think you'll see complexity and generality rise together rather than trading off, the way they eventually did in vision.

astra-6.text:
I think complexity and generality are related, but they’re not the same thing. A robot can perform a very complex task in a highly controlled environment and still be very specialized. If you change the object, its position, or the tools available, the whole system may stop working.

Generality is more about how much variation the robot can handle. Even something that sounds simple, like picking up an object, becomes challenging when it has to work with unfamiliar objects, different materials, clutter, and different environments.

So when we evaluate manipulation, I think we need to ask two questions: How difficult is the task itself, and how broad is the range of conditions under which the robot can accomplish it? Increasing complexity doesn’t automatically produce generality. The interesting challenge is building capabilities that can be reused and combined, so that learning one task makes the robot better prepared for another.

sol-6.1.text:
I think complexity and generality are related, but they’re different dimensions. A task can be very complex and still be highly specialized. A robot might execute a long sequence of precise movements in one fixed environment, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it can handle a new object or a different arrangement.

Generality is more about how broadly the capability transfers. Can the robot perform the same task with unfamiliar objects, under different conditions, or with a slightly different goal? Even something that looks simple, like picking up an object, becomes challenging when you ask for that level of generality.

So I wouldn’t measure progress only by how complicated a demonstration looks. I’d also ask how much has to be redesigned when the situation changes. Ideally, we want robots to compose reusable skills to solve increasingly complex tasks, while retaining the flexibility to handle new situations.
